entries.title: The NRSC’s Spending Surges for Key Midterm Races
entries.summary: The National Republican Senatorial Committee opened the floodgates after the Supreme Court struck down limits on party committees’ coordinated spending.
entries.content:
The National Republican Senatorial Committee’s spending sharply escalated in August following the Supreme Court’s decision to strike down federal limits capping how much parties could coordinate to spend on their candidates.

The NRSC logged less than $3 million in coordinated expenditures prior to the Supreme Court’s decision on July 30. In its most recent Federal Election Commission filing, the NRSC reported spending almost $46 million for candidates across the county.

The three largest coordinated spending allocations were more than $10 million for Sen. Jon Husted in Ohio, more than $8 million for Rep. Ashley Hinson in Iowa and nearly $8 million into Michael Whatley’s Senate race in North Carolina.

The committee also spent millions on Senate races for John Sununu in New Hampshire, Mike Rogers in Michigan, Rep. Mike Collins in Georgia and Sens. Susan Collins in Maine, Dan Sullivan in Alaska and Darline Graham in South Carolina.

The NRSC listed the purpose of the expenditures as media or direct mail production.

“The NRSC entered August with a record high cash on hand and invested it in coordinated communications,” spokesperson Joanna Rodriguez told The Washington Sun. “Republicans have already booked more in coordinated media and voter contact than our counterpart even has available in cash on hand.”

The NRSC had a more than $16 million cash-on-hand advantage over the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, according to FEC filings from July.

The DSCC did not increase its spending nearly as much. It spent less than $200,000 before the Supreme Court struck down the limits, and spent just over $1 million after the ruling, according to its most recent filing.

The coordinated spending totals reported to the FEC can represent future ad reservations, vendor contracts, polling, message testing and media training, as well as anything else the committees plan with candidates ahead of Election Day.

Before the Supreme Court ruling, campaign arms like the NRSC could only make coordinated spends of up to $61,800 per House candidate (or $123,600 if the state had only one seat). On the Senate side, the limits in 2024 ranged from $123,600 to almost $3.8 million depending on each state's voting-age population.

The NRSC teamed up with Vice President JD Vance when he was a senator from Ohio to file the lawsuit against the spending limits in 2022.

Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote in the 6-3 majority opinion that spending of campaign organizations like the NRSC should be interpreted as an expression of free speech and the limits constituted a “severe infringement” on those rights.

“In light of the other meaningful prophylactic measures available to the Government, and given the severe infringement on First Amendment-protected political speech that ensues from limiting a political party’s spending in support of its candidates, we conclude that the political-party coordinated-expenditure limits are ‘disproportionate’ and are not ‘necessary’ and ‘narrowly tailored’ for the circumvention interest it seeks to protect,” Kavanaugh wrote.

He also wrote that eliminating the spending caps would allow party committees such as the NRSC to “participate more freely and compete more fully in the political process.”

entries.title: Mystics 93, Fever 77: Game Recap
entries.summary: Kiki Iriafen racked up 21 points and 14 rebounds to lead Washington to a road win.
entries.content:
INDIANAPOLIS — Kiki Iriafen scored 21 points and grabbed 14 rebounds to help the Washington Mystics beat Indiana 93-77 and pull within a game of the fifth-place Fever.

Shakira Austin added 20 points with 10 boards for the Mystics (26-16), who are one of three teams just a game behind Indiana (27-15) with two regular-season games remaining. The Fever finish with a home-and-home series on Tuesday and Thursday against the Minnesota Lynx, owners of the WNBA’s best record at 32-10.

Sonia Citron scored 16 points and just missed a double-double with nine assists. Georgia Amoore had 11 points with three 3-pointers.

The Mystics jumped out to a 34-19 lead at the end of the first quarter. They led by as many as 26 before closing the half with a 51-30 advantage. Washington was up 77-61 entering the fourth and never were threatened.

Caitlin Clark scored 25 with five assists and Kelsey Mitchell had 22 points for the Fever. But the All-WNBA backcourt shot a combined 14 of 40 from the floor, including making just 6-of-20 3-pointers.

Fever All-Star center Aliyah Boston encountered foul trouble and scored just seven points on eight shots. And Indiana's bench didn't contribute a point until Raven Johnson's jumper with 4:35 remaining in the third quarter.
entries.author: Associated Press

entries.title: Cardinals 5, Nationals 3: Game Recap
entries.summary: After building a lead, Washington gave up three runs in the eighth inning.
entries.content:
ST. LOUIS — Iván Herrera hit a pair of home runs, and Leo Bernal also homered as the St. Louis Cardinals scored three runs in the eighth inning to come from behind and beat the Washington Nationals 5-3 on Sunday.

Bernal hit his fifth homer of the season off Yovanny Cruz (0-2) after Erik Tolman walked Jordan Walker with two outs in the eighth inning.

Herrera hit his second homer of the game and 18th of the season to tie the game at 3-all after hitting a solo shot in the first inning.

It was Herrera's third career multi-homer game and second this season after going deep twice on June 13 at Minnesota.

Luis Gastelum (5-3) pitched a scoreless eighth inning for St. Louis, and Riley O’Brien pitched a perfect ninth to earn his National League-leading 38th save.

Cardinals starter Quinn Mathews allowed three runs on seven hits and two walks in a career-high seven innings.

Jake Irvin allowed two runs on three hits and had eight strikeouts in 5 1/3 innings for the Nationals.

Brady House singled to right field to leadoff the sixth inning, and Abrams hit his 37th homer of the season to right field to put Washington ahead 3-2. He has 99 RBIs on the season.

The Nationals had a chance to add on when Daylen Lile hit a double down the right field line, but Jordan Walker delivered a perfect throw to third base to retire Lile on a call that was confirmed after Washington manager Blake Butera challenged.

entries.title: All-DMV High School Football Players of Week 4
entries.summary: This weekend’s standouts include a bounce-back star from Quince Orchard and a skilled sophomore from Digital Pioneers Academy.
entries.content:
This story is part of The Washington Sun’s All-DMV coverage. All-DMV is a new collaboration between The Sun, Fox5 DC, NBC4 Washington and WTOP News, aimed at covering the D.C. area’s best high school athletes. This week, we’ll have a volleyball players of the week story on Wednesday, and boys and girls soccer selections Friday. You can find past players of the week and more information about All-DMV here. 

With another slate of football games in the books, here are five players who turned in memorable performances in Week 4:

Jaiden Hebron, Senior, Running Back, Quince Orchard

One year ago, Hebron suffered a torn ACL in Quince Orchard’s cross-state showdown against Virginia power Stone Bridge. Now fully recovered, the senior shined in this year’s meeting with the Bulldogs, posting a 127-yard rushing performance as the Cougars extended their yearslong winning streak to 30 games with a 20-6 victory. Hebron burst free for a 42-yard dash late in the fourth quarter, then punched in a short touchdown run moments later to put the game out of reach.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Deylen Jones, Senior, Athlete, Oakton

Oakton’s 4-0 start has become one of Virginia’s most intriguing storylines early this season. The Cougars’ high-powered offense is averaging over 44 points per game and picked up a 32-23 win over Colonial Forge on Friday. Jones, a Harvard commit, has helped power Oakton’s success — the senior eclipsed 200 scrimmage yards and found the end zone four times in Friday’s victory.

Davien Parks, Senior, Linebacker, Anacostia

In Anacostia’s battle for the Southeast Cup against D.C. rival Ballou, Parks delivered a statement performance. The senior linebacker registered five sacks in a 38-0 blowout win as coach Seneca Surles’ team picked up its third straight win after dropping its season opener to Digital Pioneers. Anacostia avenged last year’s 50-0 loss to Ballou with a shutout performance of its own.

Kenaz Sullivan, Senior, Defensive Back, The St. James

The young Strivers, a second-year program loaded with Division I commits, have played as advertised through the first month of the season. Coach Darryl Overton’s team thumped Mount Zion Prep on Friday, 65-0. Sullivan, a four-star Maryland commit, pulled down two interceptions in the victory. The Strivers will look to Sullivan for more defensive fireworks with matchups looming against national powers IMG Academy and St. Frances.

Laroy Williams, Sophomore, Running Back, Digital Pioneers

Williams rushed for 182 yards and three touchdowns on just eight carries as the Pythons handled H.D. Woodson this week, 34-0. The win was a resilient performance for Digital Pioneers, which squandered an early 16-point lead to Theodore Roosevelt last week. With their sophomore running back leading the charge on offense, the Pythons look to contend for the city crown following an 11-win season last year.
entries.author: Noah Ferguson

entries.title: NFL Week 2 Takeaways: What’s Wrong With The Chargers?
entries.summary: Plus, the Bears had a scary Sunday and Ja’Marr Chase made the play of the day.
entries.content:
The second Sunday of the NFL season featured a few key injuries, an early contender for catch of the year and another win from a capable backup. Here are five takeaways from Week 2:

It was a nightmarish day for the Bears. 

On Friday, the Bears proudly proclaimed on X that the team had a clean injury report for the first time since Week 7 of the 2022 season. That luck changed on Sunday.

The Bears lost quarterback Caleb Williams halfway through the fourth quarter of a 9–3 home defeat against the Vikings. Williams, a D.C. native who starred at Gonzaga, went down without contact in the fourth quarter and had to be helped off the field after trying to walk off under his own power.

Bears coach Ben Johnson said after the game that Williams injured his right hamstring and the team will know more on Monday after he undergoes testing.

“I'm actually happy it's nothing with the knee,” Johnson said. “That was my first inclination. But yeah, a hamstring can be pretty damaging as well. We'll see how bad it is tomorrow and we'll go from there. Quickly, you've got to turn the page.”

The injury capped off a rough day for the Bears’ offense. After hanging a franchise-record 59 points on the Panthers last week, Chicago struggled to get anything going against Minnesota. The Vikings’ defense made Williams uncomfortable with constant pressure and finished with three sacks.

Tyson Bagent, Chicago’s backup, went 5 for 9 for 54 yards after replacing Williams. The Bears host the Eagles for Monday Night Football in Week 3, giving Williams an extra day to recover if tests show he can play next week.

Ja’Marr Chase made a highlight grab to keep the Bengals rolling. 

It’s way too early to declare a catch of the year, but Bengals wideout Ja’Marr Chase submitted a strong early candidate on Sunday. Late in the first half of the Bengals’ 20–6 win over the Texans, Chase spun off his defender and hauled in a 32-yard pass, planting his toes in the front corner to the endzone. The highlight grab marked the first of his two touchdowns on the day as Cincinnati moved to 2-0.

https://x.com/NFLonCBS/status/2101736151983816836

“I literally don’t know what I did,” Chase said of the catch. “I couldn’t see the ball for a second and I was fighting just trying to get in position, but by the time I’d seen the ball it was in the light and it came real fast and was an adjustment.”

The Bengals went 6–11 last year in the organization’s first losing season since 2020. Joe Burrow, who missed nine games in 2025 with a toe injury, has emphasized the importance of this season and getting the Bengals back to the playoffs. So far, the team’s offense is clicking and a revamped defense has fared well. Despite losing star pass rusher Trey Hendrickson to the Ravens in free agency, the unit has eight sacks through two games.

What’s wrong with the Chargers? 

Los Angeles was a popular preseason pick to make a deep playoff run this year, especially after it brought in Mike McDaniel as offensive coordinator. But McDaniels’ marriage with quarterback Justin Herbert is off to a rocky start. After a 26-14 loss to the Raiders Sunday, the Chargers are 0-2. It’s the first time in Jim Harbaugh’s head coaching career that one of his teams, college or pro, has started 0-2.

Through two games, Herbert has more interceptions than touchdowns (3 to 2) and his offense is averaging just 14 points per game. Even with young playmakers like running back Omarion Hampton and wide receivers Ladd McConkey and Quentin Johnston, Herbert and McDaniels have struggled to get the unit going.

After Sunday’s game, Herbert called his play "uncharacteristic” and added the team has practiced better than it’s played.

“That’s not good enough and we can’t expect to win games like that when we’re playing like that,” he said. “If we’re not playing up to our standard, that’s on us to fix it.”

With the Bills, Seahawks, Broncos and Chiefs all on the horizon, the Chargers suddenly have little margin for error.

Trey Smack AP - 26263747989274 (5488x3659, AR: 1.50)
The Eagles and Packers had to sweat it out. 

The Titans came close to pulling off the day’s biggest upset. Jalen Hurts found Darius Cooper for a three-yard touchdown with nine seconds left in regulation to lift the Eagles to a 24–20 comeback win in Tennessee. It was a positive ending to a bad day for Hurts, who threw two interceptions and was sacked three times.

Saquon Barkley rushed for just nine yards on four carries after injuring his left arm on the Eagles’ first offensive play of the day. He returned in the third quarter to help Philadelphia fend off the Titans. A field goal gave Tennessee a three-point lead with 1:56 left, but Hurts led the Eagles 62 yards in eight plays to set up the game-winning touchdown.

In New York, another NFC contender was put to the test as the Packers needed overtime to earn a 20-17 win over the Jets. Green Bay trailed 17–7 with 11 minutes left in the fourth quarter before scoring 13 unanswered points to improve to 2–0. Jordan Love threw for two touchdown passes, and rookie Trey Smack (another DMV native) hit the game-winning field goal in overtime to deny the Jets an upset.

“It’s one of those games where you just have to keep fighting,” Love said after the game. “It wasn’t pretty, a lot of that game.”

The Packers were without Micah Parsons, who is still rehabbing an ACL tear he suffered late last season. Two more players joined the injury report Sunday as wide receiver Jayden Reed and right tackle Zach Bako-Bewele went down on consecutive plays. Bako-Bewele injured his knee and didn’t return. Reed injured his neck and was hospitalized, but the team said after the game he has feeling in his extremities.

“Doing much better,” Reed posted to X. “Appreciate all the prayers and support.”

Drew Lock kept the defending champs on track. 

Sam who? The defending champions are 2–0 despite the fact that Sam Darnold has played just five snaps this year. With Darnold sidelined by a glute injury, backup Drew Lock has kept the Seahawks flying. On Sunday, he threw three touchdowns to Jaxon Smith-Njigba in a 31–7 win over the Cardinals.

The Seahawks’ defense seems to have picked up where it left off last year, surrendering just two touchdowns in two games with five sacks and four interceptions.

Lock has completed 73% of his passes, throwing for 422 yards, four touchdowns and zero interceptions. His play has given the Seahawks some leeway with Darnold’s recovery. Seahawks coach Mike Macdonald said on Sunday that Darnold could return to practice as early as this week, but with Seattle facing the winless Commanders and Chargers over the next two weeks there may not be reason to hurry.
entries.author: Alex Schiffer

entries.title: Farmers Are 'Pissed' Over Trump's Moves on Beef and Tariffs
entries.summary: The president has upset a reliably Republican rural voter base ahead of the midterms.
entries.content:
Ryan Marquardt, the vice president of the Iowa Farmers Union, was working at an Iowa State Fair booth when the news broke that the U.S. would import hundreds of thousands of tons of below-market-priced beef from Argentina and Brazil.

“I’ve never seen farmers more pissed,” Marquardt said. “That was the maddest I’ve seen farmers in a long time.”

The decision was one of several actions by the Trump administration that experts and insiders say have dulled enthusiasm for Republicans among rural voters, who are already facing high input costs from the war in Iran and escalating trade wars with some of the country’s biggest buyers of American agriculture.

Republicans also control Congress, but have struggled to pass a long-awaited farm bill that farmers say is desperately needed.

Republicans have relied on rural voters to form a solid piece of their base in recent elections, and some argue that the Democratic brand is too poor to rehabilitate in many areas. However, experts still see rural voter apathy as a major issue for Republicans. Even if it doesn't chip away at a crucial voting bloc in some key statewide races this cycle, it could cost the party down the road in a post-Donald Trump future. 

“A lot of people who are now being called ‘reliable Republican voters’ weren’t within living memory,” said William A. Galston, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution.

“It takes something big to change long-established voting patterns, but I think there’s a possibility that the Trump administration has done things that are big enough and bad enough from the standpoint of rural America to make some of the voters who shifted a decade ago reconsider their choice,” Galston said.

Trump’s decision in August to import beef was meant to lower prices, but it sent a shock through American ranchers, who are at their lowest herd counts in decades. Beef prices have risen to record highs, and many producers have begun the long process of rebuilding their herds to meet demand.

Trump also entered an increasingly escalating trade war in August with Canada, a major trading partner. Canada is one of the largest buyers of American agriculture, and experts expect the country to seek imports elsewhere if tariffs make American products too costly.

“Our economies are intertwined on purpose,” John Hansen, the president of the Nebraska Farmers Union, said. “You cannot shoot either Canada or Mexico in the foot without your own foot bleeding.”

Trump’s approval rating fell by 22 percentage points among rural voters from July to August, before his administration announced its intention to import 300,000 pounds of beef and Canada responded with its own tariffs on American goods.

Galston believes that recent data shows a depressed Republican electorate in rural America, one that is still looking for the end of the war in Iran and relief from trade wars that have raised the costs of importing essential materials and made it more expensive to trade in foreign markets.

“He keeps on promising that things are going to get better abruptly,” Galston said. “The timing of the abrupt shift for the better keeps on getting pushed backward, but the shape of the promise remains the same. Eat your spinach today, and there'll be ice cream tomorrow. I think people are no longer willing to believe that.”

Experts and insiders say that the president’s unpopular policies have put races in play in states that Trump carried by double digits in 2024. One Republican consultant who was granted anonymity to discuss campaign discussions pointed to Iowa, where Democrats have leads or remain close in polling across the Senate, governor’s and House races, despite Trump winning Iowa by 13 percentage points in 2024.

The Senate race remains close in Kansas as well, albeit with a Republican advantage, where Trump won by 16 percentage points in 2024. Democrats also lead in polls for the Ohio Senate race, where Trump won by 11 percentage points.

“Rural Americans are feeling the pinch just like everybody else is,” the Republican insider said. “Anytime you raise the cost of goods, that's a bad thing, and so it's going to have an impact on voter apathy or voter excitement.”

Trump’s decisions have sparked backlash among Republicans in both chambers of Congress.

“I’m extremely disappointed by this decision from the White House,” Sen. Deb Fischer (R-Nebraska) said on X. “We all want lower grocery prices, but as I’ve said for months, we cannot do it at the expense of American producers. Flooding the market with foreign beef hurts our livestock industry and undermines the long-term solution: growing the U.S. cattle herd to meet demand.”

Other Republicans, including Sens. Jerry Moran of Kansas, Susan Collins of Maine, Mike Rounds of South Dakota and Thom Tillis of North Carolina, as well as Rep. Ron Estes of Kansas, have all spoken out against importing new foreign beef, the new tariffs with Canada or both.

Sen. Jim Risch (R-Idaho), a cattle rancher, spoke out against the White House’s showing interest in importing Argentinian beef a year ago, saying, “If you flood the market, that hurts beef producers badly.”

The Trump administration has tried to tamp down the backlash.

Trump announced an executive order that would give producers additional authority to process and sell their own product, in an attempt to challenge the hold the four largest meat processors have on the industry. Some industry insiders weren’t satisfied with the exchange.

“For us, it feels a little bit more like it's a Band-Aid for a very different kind of wound,” said Jenna Stanton, a policy director for Western Skies Strategies.

Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins has acknowledged the impact of importing beef on America’s ranchers, telling Fox News in an interview that she first heard the news while on her way to Iowa.

“In a way, that was a blessing, because that way I could work to explain the president’s thinking but also hear directly from the ranchers just how difficult that decision was,” Rollins said.

Rollins has had to balance Trump’s desire for lower food prices during an election year when affordability concerns have become a top issue for voters, with an agriculture sector in desperate need of a profit margin.

Rollins has said she believes the current prices for American-produced ground beef are reasonable, but prices still need to go down. On Thursday, she announced a plan for mandatory country-of-origin labeling in part to “protect the American rancher.”

Republicans in Congress are also struggling to use their majority to pass farm policy, most notably the first full five-year farm bill since 2018. The bill advanced from the Senate Agriculture Committee on a party-line vote Wednesday, but its fate on the floor remains uncertain amid a partisan divide over payment shifts in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program.

Congress hasn’t passed an updated farm bill since 2018 and has relied on extensions since then to keep essential farm programs running. Farmers are desperate for updated commodity reference prices, which haven’t been updated since inflation worsened after the COVID-19 pandemic.

Trump also took to Truth Social to reaffirm his commitment to passing a farm bill, saying much-needed financial assistance would be on the way. “I want to totally reassure our Farmers and Ranchers, and our Rural Communities, that they will be extremely happy with the end result,” he said.

Weeks before Election Day, Republicans now have to pitch a mixed bag of policies to voters who increasingly view the Trump administration unfavorably. This unfavorability toward Trump may not benefit Democrats, experts say.

Nicholas Jacobs, a professor of American government at Colby College in Maine who has written a book on the voting habits of rural Americans, thinks Democrats have a unique opportunity to make inroads with communities of voters they’ve lost, but isn’t optimistic they will.

“They call the Democratic Party the big tent party,” Jacobs said. “Sometimes I wonder if there’s still room for rural people in that big tent.”
entries.author: Tyler Spence

entries.title: Germany Is Paying the Price for Trump’s EU Feud
entries.summary: Trump’s escalating tariff threats and Chinese competition are crushing Europe’s top exporting country.
entries.content:
BERLIN — Germany’s postwar economy was built for export, but now it’s taking a sizable hit.

U.S. tariffs imposed by President Donald Trump are hurting the sales of the cars and machinery that previously made Germany the most powerful economy in the European Union. Chinese manufacturing competitors are outpacing German companies. And with energy costs rising because of the Iran war, economic analysts and German officials fear the country could slip into a recession.

Feeling the economic strain, some German voters are turning to the political fringes for candidates who promise change, while the country’s leaders — including German Chancellor Friedrich Merz — work to prove they can turn the economy around.

“We’ve seen a longer period of barely any economic growth for a couple of years,” said Melanie Vogelbach, head of international economic policy at the German Chamber of Commerce and Industry.

Vogelbach called for the German government to address increasing regulatory bureaucracy, an aging population and the rising costs of labor and energy to jump-start the stagnated economy.

“We do have to remember that we do have a lot of structural problems at home that are not necessarily only related to international developments,” Vogelbach said, pointing to high costs, heavy tax burdens and what she called “excessive bureaucracy” that slows down projects and permitting.

As one of the biggest exporters of automotive and manufacturing globally, Germany faces particularly acute economic problems. The Kiel Institute for the World Economy estimated that automotive and manufacturing tariffs levied by the United States could cost the German economy billions in output in the short term.

Experts say the effects of a worsening economy in Germany reveal how much European economies depend on U.S. cooperation. U.S. tariffs have significantly affected German exports, with most German goods facing a 15% baseline tariff, while steel and aluminum are subject to a 50% levy.

The issue came to a head this week when the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, addressed issues with the United States. Speaking to the European Parliament on Wednesday, she said transatlantic relationships faced a “fracture in the international rules-based system.” Von der Leyen also proposed the EU expand its trade agreement with Canada and potentially make it the first associate member of the bloc.

Trump responded by threatening to levy “very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe.”

He added: “If it’s a good intention, that’s fine. If it’s a bad intention, we’ll put very heavy tariffs on Europe.”

The German chancellor unveiled a sweeping economic reform package called "Programme for Revival and Employment" on July 2 that aimed to resuscitate Germany's economy by easing bureaucratic burdens and boosting labor market competitiveness. As Germans go to the polls in the coming months, it remains an open question if Merz will emerge with a governing coalition that could pass the economic package.

The stagnant economy appears to be spurring German voters to turn toward far-right parties, such as Alternative for Germany, to solve rising costs, decreasing job opportunities and the slowdown in economic growth.

"When you are worried about your future, when you're worried about having your job in the future, that is something that mostly triggers you or makes you at least open to vote extreme, maybe out of protest," Simon Schütz, a spokesperson for the German Association of the Automotive Industry, told the Washington Sun.

He added: "If you don't take those tough decisions now, you might have to take much tougher decisions in some time. The goal is to work together to make the business model in Germany fit for the future once again. Only in this way will we be able to continue manufacturing here. And only in this way can we safeguard jobs."

Rolf J. Langhammer, a researcher at the Kiel Institute, placed China’s rise in economic power within a broader list of pressures facing Germany: an aging population, lagging digitalization and artificial intelligence adoption relative to the U.S. and China, as well as an incomplete shift to renewable energy.

“Germany, and also the European Union, but Germany in particular, is an aging economy which has profound changes in its production structure, in its demand structure,’ he said.

Schütz framed the tariffs as one more strain on an automotive industry already losing its competitive footing.

"When you look at certain location-side factors such as energy prices, bureaucracy, taxes, regulation — all of this, Europe has kind of lost its base, and other regions went ahead of it," Schütz said.

Langhammer said German lawmakers and officials must figure out how to move forward without relying on the United States.

“Europe must become economically more independent,” Langhammer said, “and rely on its own strength.”

entries.title: Bessent Says the U.S. Is Pushing China for an AI Incident Alert System
entries.summary: The Treasury secretary said he discussed the matter with Chinese officials.
entries.content:
By Matt Sedensky

NEW YORK — Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday the U.S. has proposed a new “notification mechanism” for artificial intelligence incidents that could affect national security, part of weekend discussions ahead of talks at the White House this week between President Donald Trump and China’s Xi Jinping.

“We want a shared vision of common goals and common threats,” Bessent told reporters after talks with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng in New York. “We think that just like any cross-border activity, that moving from opaque to more transparency between the No. 1 and the No. 2 AI powers in the world is very important.”

Trump has resisted calls to slow down AI development, saying that would help China catch up to U.S. companies.

Standing together in the soaring lobby of the JPMorgan Chase headquarters late Sunday, Bessent and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the groundwork had been laid for talks between Xi and Trump set to take place on Thursday. They said the two sides had agreed to operationalize a new “Board of Trade” that the two leaders had discussed when they met in Beijing in May.

“Today those notions have become reality,” Greer said.

Greer said the countries were still discussing what “nonsensitive” items could be considered for lower tariffs, but that the list could potentially include consumer and agricultural goods, energy products and medical devices.

Chinese state media Xinhua said Bessent and the vice premier talked about issues “relating to AI” without mentioning specifics and also had “candid, in-depth and constructive” discussions on key economic and trade issues.

“The fact that both sides agreed to continue the dialogue is significant,” said George Chen, a partner and chair of digital practice at The Asia Group consultancy, in written comments. “The initial outcome — an AI risk notification mechanism — sets a precedent that other countries may follow.”

___
Chan Ho-him in Hong Kong and Huizhong Wu in Bangkok contributed to this report.

entries.title: CNN, MS NOW and Politico Say They're Suing Over Trump's Ban
entries.summary: The president said he was barring journalists from all three outlets over "fake news."
entries.content:
CNN, MS NOW and Politico said Monday they’ve notified President Donald Trump’s administration that they’re filing a lawsuit over being denied White House access.

Reporters from the three major news organizations were blocked from the White House on Saturday, a day after Trump said he was barring them because of reporting he found to be “fake news.”

The actions were a clear escalation of Trump’s long-running efforts — in the courts and through administrative action — to restrict news coverage by journalists he finds objectionable and were the latest test of First Amendment protections in the United States. Trump had said Friday he would ban all three outlets because of coverage he disliked.

White House reporters from the two cable networks — Betsy Klein of CNN and Akayla Gardner of MS NOW — went live to report they’d been turned away, their press badges deactivated, when arriving for their jobs at the White House. Soon after, Politico said its White House reporter Cheyenne Haslett was also denied entry and had her badge confiscated.

All three news outlets had hinted at legal action, saying they would vigorously defend their First Amendment rights.

“Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists' credentials because it objected to our reporting,” the outlets said in a joint statement posted on X. “Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference.”

In his second term, Trump and his Republican administration have upped the ante and punished certain media outlets, both in the courtroom and through regulatory action. Trump has also lashed out at individual reporters in person or over social media, sometimes in strikingly personal terms — insulting them in briefings or in his recent speech at the White House Correspondents’ Association dinner.

The WHCA’s president, Jacqui Heinrich, called on the Trump administration to immediately restore the three outlets’ access. “The implications extend beyond these organizations: a standard used to exclude one news outlet because of its coverage could be applied to any outlet in the future,” Heinrich said. “The American people, through a free and independent press, must be able to scrutinize those elected to power, regardless of whether government officials view it favorably.”

entries.content:
Good morning. This is The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for Sept. 21, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

In today’s newsletter: A “crisis” for D.C’s courts, ammunition in Trump’s arch and an injured Jayden Daniels.

Capital Weather’s Daily Digit: 7/10. Hello 70s, goodbye 80s. Lots of clouds, maybe a passing shower. Read the full forecast.

THE LATEST

Lobbying is intensifying around what many say is a growing crisis in D.C.’s courts — and the significant role that Congress has had in creating it.

More than 300 groups and individuals in D.C. have written to the U.S. Senate, urging members to reverse a proposed 13% cut to the current year’s budget — which itself has remained flat for the last four years, even as civil and domestic case filings jumped 33% and criminal cases have spiked 160%.

“As the number of criminal prosecutions and civil matters rise even more sharply, the D.C. Courts are under severe strain to meet the needs of the District’s residents and visitors,” reads the letter, which was spearheaded by the D.C. Council for Court Excellence.

Unlike any other state-based court system, D.C.’s judiciary — composed of D.C. Superior Court and the D.C. Court of Appeals, akin to the city’s supreme court — are solely funded by Congress. The U.S. Senate also plays another critical role: It confirms presidential nominations for judgeship.

Persistent judicial vacancies were often the rallying cry for D.C. officials and advocates; they said that empty judgeships meant the gears of justice moved much more slowly, especially as caseloads increased. In August, the Senate acted on a number of pending nominations, giving the Court of Appeals its first full slate of judges in years.

Those same advocates are now pushing for increased funding for the 2027 fiscal year, which starts on Oct. 1. The chief judges of both Superior Court and the Court of Appeals have also made the appeal directly, writing in an August op-ed that “the D.C. courts have reached a fiscal breaking point.”

“Every arrest, hearing, mediation, and trial depends on a court system with enough people and resources to process cases fairly and on time. Adding judges while cutting the infrastructure that supports them would undermine the progress Congress just made,” said Misty Thomas Zaleski, executive director of the Council for Court Excellence.

Will Congress listen? The House is already gone and won’t return until after the November midterm elections, while the Senate will be out of town for almost all of October. Still, lawmakers face a December deadline to agree to a new federal budget for 2027, including funding for D.C.’s courts.

FROM THE COURTHOUSE

Council member Trayon White’s bribery trial could wrap up this week. The prosecutors and defense rested their respective cases on Friday.

White stands accused of accepting bribes from former government contractor Allieu Kamara, who during the summer of 2024 was acting as a government informant. The government alleges that White, in exchange for the money, promised to use his position as D.C. Council member to help steer more government grants toward Kamara’s companies, Life Deeds and District Services Management.

Some of the key witnesses on Friday included Office of Neighborhood Safety and Engagement Director Kwelli Sneed and former D.C. Attorney General Karl Racine. The Washington Sun’s Jenny Gathright reports that Sneed testified about a meeting White had with her in July 2024, but she said that while White did bring up Life Deeds, he never pressured her to renew the company’s government grants.

Racine said he had “absolutely no recollection” of White approaching him concerning pending litigation involving Life Deeds. That testimony was important because Kamara had previously testified about bribing White as he sought the council member’s help resolving a contract dispute.

Kevin Searby, one of White’s attorneys, told the judge on Friday that the government’s case was a “hot mess.” Prosecutors had not brought enough evidence to show that his client made any serious agreement with Kamara to influence government grants, he argued.

Prosecutors said that it doesn’t matter whether White actually took any significant steps to steer government contracts towards Kamara. All that matters, Assistant U.S. Attorney Rebecca Ross said, is that White agreed to do so — she argued the evidence shows he did.

The lawyers will meet today to hash out some remaining questions with Judge Rudolph Contreras, and the jury will return to court on Tuesday.

FROM THE DISTRICT

Just add water. The Smithsonian Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden installed a new sculpture last week: a 28-foot-tall pool by artist duo Elmgreen & Dragset. The sculpture garden will reopen Oct. 31 following a four-year renovation.

The Department of Defense has bought 2,000 unlimited, flat-rate “public service” Metro passes for D.C. National Guard members to be used through Jan. 31, 2029, according to a contract reviewed by The Sun. The benefit is available to all federal departments and agencies at a cost of $144 per month per participating employee.

President Donald Trump said his proposed arch between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery would double as a “top grade military complex,” housing “large numbers” of drones and snipers while storing ammunition, the Associated Press reports. In an X post, Rep. Don Beyer (D-Virginia) called the idea “stupid, dangerous, and unworkable” given how close the arch would be to National Airport’s airspace.

Last week, an official in D.C.’s Historic Preservation Office called on Trump to scrap his arch for a smaller monument, The Sun’s Kendall Staton reports.

D.C.’s State Board of Education unanimously approved new graduation requirements last week, WUSA9 reports. The new standards add a financial literacy requirement, reduce community service hours and expand how world language credits are obtained. The board also approved an additional integrated math course.

Don’t expect to see a lot of happy faces in a D.C.-area airport. The region’s three airports each ranked below average in a new customer satisfaction survey from analytics company J.D. Power, Staton reports.

Former board members of the United States Institute of Peace filed an emergency plea to a federal court late Thursday to stop Trump’s name being affixed onto its headquarters, The Sun’s Angie Orellana Hernandez reports. It mirrors the ongoing legal battle at the Kennedy Center, where around 1,000 people showed up Friday to protest Trump’s reshaping of the storied arts hub, The Sun’s Torrie Herrington reports.

FROM VIRGINIA

Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger signed an executive order on Friday implementing a “data center accountability framework” that would ban the use of non-disclosure agreements that have made it harder for the public to follow proposed developments, expedite development of noise regulations, and direct a review of diesel and other backup generators used to power data centers, The Sun’s Taylor Giorno reports.

FROM MARYLAND

Montgomery County’s police chief abruptly resigned Friday after two years in the role, The Sun’s Justice Covert reports. Marc Yamada resigned just before the county inspector general released an investigation into alleged misconduct by an unnamed police department executive. County Executive Marc Elrich suggested it was Yamada, who previously faced whistleblower complaints about his use of funds on a trip to Las Vegas.

TRIVIA

Aside from John F. Kennedy, who is the only other president buried at Arlington National Cemetery? 
  1. Theodore Roosevelt 
  2. Ulysses S. Grant
  3. William Howard Taft
Email us your answer — the first reader who gets it right will receive a shout-out at the end of tomorrow’s newsletter.

SPORTS

Cowboys 37, Commanders 20: On the final play of the first half in Dallas, Washington lost its quarterback and its momentum. Trailing by a touchdown and facing a third-and-goal from Dallas’ 1-yard line, Jayden Daniels stumbled out of a snap and injured his left elbow in the fall. It’s the same elbow that kept him out for several games last season. Without him, Washington struggled to recalibrate in the second half of an ugly Week 2 loss.

  • Martenzie Johnson breaks down Daniels’ injury and the moment that changed the game. 
  • Dave Sheinin writes about the larger impact of Sunday’s loss. Is Washington’s season over after two weeks? 
  • And Alex Schiffer rounds up the biggest Sunday storylines from the rest of the league.
The Mystics made a statement against Caitlin Clark and the Fever on Sunday, earning a 93-77 win in Indiana. Kiki Iriafen led the way with 21 points and 14 rebounds as Washington poured in 34 first-quarter points and never looked back.

The Sun is starting something new to cover high school sports. All-DMV is a collaboration between The Sun, Fox5 DC, NBC4 Washington and WTOP News, aimed at covering the D.C. area’s best high school athletes. Each week, The Sun’s Noah Ferguson will choose standout performers in football (Mondays), volleyball (Wednesdays) and boys and girls soccer (Fridays). This week’s football selections include a four-star Maryland commit and a sophomore star.

What to Watch Today

MLB: Nationals at Tigers, 6:40 p.m. (MLB.TV)
NFL: Giants at Rams, 8:15 p.m. (ESPN)

entries.title: Trump's World Stage Awaits
entries.content:
Today’s notice: A foreign affairs test awaits Trump in New York. The anti-corruption script coming to your TV. How U.S. policies are affecting Germany’s right turn. And: Farm country ain’t happy with Trump.  


THE LATEST

Ahead of Donald Trump’s address to the United Nations this week, the president posted an image of himself peering over a globe that includes Greenland and the Arctic Circle but with his gaze seemingly centered on Europe. “His Hemisphere,” the text over the image reads, as though he is staking a claim to the northern half of the world.

It was apropos, perhaps, to the moment as the world awaits Trump’s actions on a host of Earth-defining crises, including the war in Iran, the 4-year-old Russia-Ukraine war, ballistic missiles just launched from North Korea and a friendly visit from the leader of China to Washington while the two superpowers continue to grapple economically, especially in an AI race.

As nearly 130 world leaders assemble in New York for this week's U.N. General Assembly, Trump has the chance to lay out his foreign policy agenda at a uniquely frustrating period in his second term. A senior U.S. official said the president plans to highlight the “peace deals that he has driven to conclusion or is in the process of driving to conclusion,” as well as many issues “frankly neglected by past administrations.”

Topping the list: Iran. Over the weekend, the president questioned when it was time to “blow the entire nation up” but also expressed willingness to meet with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian while at the U.N.

Trump speaks Tuesday, and will also hold face-to-face meetings with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, acting Venezuelan President Delcy Rodríguez, the heads of state for U.S. allies in the Middle East and the person Trump calls the “communist” leader of New York City, Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

One foreign leader will get his own high-profile summit with Trump. Chinese President Xi Jinping and Trump will be back in Washington on Wednesday with an arrival ceremony, a state dinner Thursday and a tour of the National Archives on the schedule.

More: Trump Says His Planned Arch Would Also Become a ‘Military Complex’ • Trump Pledges to Appoint an ‘AI Czar’ as He Defends the Technology • Trump Says U.S. Will Have ‘Permanent Control’ Over Military Presence In Greenland

Open tabs:

  • Trump asked budget chief to draft order bringing health research funding under his control (Politico)
  • Secret contracts reveal undisclosed terms in Trump’s drug-pricing deals (WaPo)
  • Trump Ramps Up Bid to Dismantle International Criminal Court (WSJ)
  • How President Trump Broke the Kennedy Center (NYT)




FROM THE WHITE HOUSE


Or more accurately, from outside the White House: MS NOW hosted live shots on the corner of 17th and Pennsylvania Avenue yesterday after the network’s team was barred from entering the Northwest Gate, as were journalists from Politico and CNN. Trump threatened to add more outlets to his banned list, including The Washington Post and The New York Times.

House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-Louisiana) said on ABC’s “This Week” that he didn’t know why the president blocked the outlets but touted Trump as the most open-to-the-press president on record. When pressed on whether the ban violated the Constitution, Sen. John Barrasso (R-Wyoming) said on NBC’s “Meet the Press”— multiple times — that he believes “the press has an obligation to report fairly” and he doesn’t think it will have an impact on the coming midterms.

The president of the White House Correspondents’ Association, Fox News’ Jacqui Henrich, talked yesterday with her predecessor, CBS News’ Weijia Jiang.

“Let's be very clear: It is an absolute privilege to cover the White House and the president, and we don't take that for granted,” Jiang said. “But when you start selecting who's allowed to do that, the viewpoint shrinks.”

FROM THE CAMPAIGN TRAIL


Everyone’s running against corruption: It’s becoming the central line of attack in the 2026 midterms, The Sun’s Elena Schneider and Alex Roarty report, with both parties and their allies spending millions on ads employing the topic as their main cudgel.

The ads follow a similar script: Costs are rising because the opposing politician is taking donations from special interests, which then receive the green light to raise prices on utilities, health care, etc., etc., while the politician turns a blind eye, Elena and Alex write. Democrats generally don’t name-check Trump in their ads. (We explored one reason why last year.) Republican spots are designed to do this: “Your job is to remind Republican voters, who are depressed in these red districts and states, that these candidates are unacceptable alternatives,” GOP pollster Robert Blizzard said.

First on The Sun: mobilizing natural disaster survivors. Tides, a progressive mega-spending group, is funding a new nationwide effort aimed at mobilizing voters in states affected by recent deadly weather events as scientists say human-caused climate change is making extreme weather more common. The nonprofit Extreme Weather Survivors launches the push today, and plans to hold events in states affected by extreme weather: North Carolina, Texas, Colorado and California, according to a release shared with The Sun. The goal is to “engage and motivate survivors of disasters ahead of the midterm election.”

FROM GERMANY


Facing recession from U.S. policy choices: Trump’s tariffs and the energy price spikes caused by the war in Iran are battering Europe’s most powerful economy, The Sun’s Daniella Diaz reports from Berlin. German companies are also falling behind their Chinese competitors, and the stagnant economy is spurring German voters to turn toward far-right parties, Daniella writes. The German government is trying to adapt, but is limited in what it can do because of the nation’s dependence on American markets. “Europe must become economically more independent,” Rolf J. Langhammer, a researcher at the Kiel Institute, told The Sun.

FROM THE REDISTRICTING WARS


After the new lines: “I think they made a miscalculation about what the impact of them doing this actually will mean for them.” That’s the take from Ashley Shelton, a Louisiana organizer focused on Black voters, about Republican lawmakers in the state who successfully redrew district lines after the Supreme Court’s Callais decision. The Sun’s Adora Brown reports on efforts across the redistricted South to drive up Black turnout in protest, and make the new gerrymandered seats less of a foregone conclusion.





NEW ON THE WASHINGTON SUN

Farmers’ beef with Trump: Farmers and the Republicans who represent most of farm country in Congress are increasingly vocal in their frustration with White House moves to import foreign beef and continue with tariffs that affect the export markets they rely on. The Sun’s Tyler Spence takes a deep dive into the political fallout in places Republicans generally count on in statewide contests. “Rural Americans are feeling the pinch just like everybody else is,” a Republican insider said. “Anytime you raise the cost of goods, that's a bad thing, and so it's going to have an impact on voter apathy or voter excitement.”



Some doubt this is a situation Democrats can actually take advantage of. The party’s standing in these parts of the country remains not great. “They call the Democratic Party the big tent party,” Nicholas Jacobs, a Colby College professor who is an expert on rural politics, told Tyler. “Sometimes I wonder if there’s still room for rural people in that big tent.”



More: Activists Rally to Reopen Kennedy Center As Its Future Remains Uncertain • An ICE Shooting Wounds a Man in Austin, Texas • The NRSC’s Spending Surges for Key Midterm Races





NOT US

  • The Company Trump Can’t Ignore, by Sophia Cai and Cheyenne Haslett for Politico
  • On the Shores of Trump’s Lake America, It’s Still Lake Ontario, by Maya Davis for The Wall Street Journal
  • Trump’s Census Proposal Could Cut House Seats From Red States, by Jeff Adelson and Albert Sun for The New York Times
  • How the surging cost of going out is changing American life, by Julie Z. Weil and Miriam Waldvogel for The Washington Post




WEEK AHEAD 


Today 

Trump heads to New York City for the U.N. General Assembly and meets with Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

JD Vance visits North Carolina.

Tuesday 

Kamala Harris campaigns with Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan.

Wednesday 

President Xi Jinping arrives in Washington.

A Senate Judiciary subcommittee holds a hearing on Flock cameras and AI surveillance.

Thursday 

Trump hosts a state dinner for Xi.

The Senate HELP Committee holds a hearing to consider Heidi Overton’s nomination to be FDA commissioner.

Saturday

Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito speaks at Pepperdine Law School in Malibu and Justice Brett Kavanaugh speaks at the St. Thomas More Society dinner in Dallas.

The newsletter was produced by Thomas Burr, Nikie Johnson and Gaby Morera Di Núbila.

entries.title: Southern Organizers Bet Redistricting Will Fuel Democrats
entries.summary: Black voters hope to be “too big to rig,” organizers say.
entries.content:
Voting rights organizers in Southern states are banking on anger over Republican redistricting to push Democrats beyond expectations come November.

Across the South, organizers are taking steps to get out the vote — organizing at block parties and arts events, as well as hosting rallies and voting drives. They’re also sending trained, nonpartisan poll monitors to districts with predominant populations of color.

Polling has found that effort could be working. Rep. Shomari Figures, whose Alabama seat was heavily redistricted, is now tied with his Republican opponent in polls from the House Majority PAC and the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee.

“If you can just change the rules anytime you want and do what you want, people feel powerless in some regard. But that is not what is happening in Memphis,” said Matia Powell, the executive director of Civic Tennessee, an organization aiming to advance civic power. “People see this as an opportunity for them to have their voices heard even more and fight back and make sure that this doesn't continue to happen.”

Tennessee’s U.S. House map was redistricted in May to split Memphis, once the seat of a Black-majority congressional district, into three other districts. Following that decision, the state’s August primaries had its largest turnout in a decade in Shelby County, which includes Memphis.

For Civic Tennessee and other organizations in the state, that outcome is the product of real effort on the ground to inform voters about the effects of redistricting. Organizers canvassed door-to-door, made phone calls and held events to educate voters on their new districts.

“We're just meeting people where they're at and making sure that they have the correct information to make appropriate decisions and cast a ballot,” Powell added.

The midterm landscape has been shifted and shaped by Republican redistricting, which has shattered formerly majority-minority districts that once held large Black voter populations.

The push is taking place across the South, including in Alabama, Louisiana and North Carolina.

The April Supreme Court decision in Louisiana v. Callais effectively stripped Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, which protected and sometimes required majority-minority districts. The loss of those protections threatens the seats of several Black incumbent lawmakers including Figures and Rep. Don Davis (D-North Carolina). Rep. Cleo Fields (D-Louisiana) decided not to run for reelection after the Callais decision eliminated his district.

“This is about Black political power,” Shayla Mitchell, an election-protection organizer in Alabama, told The Washington Sun. “Civil rights and voters' rights policy was created for Black people to have access to ballots. The way these policies and redistricting are being written now and being done are outsourcing or getting rid of Black districts.”

In North Carolina, organizers say they’re gaining momentum. North Carolina’s 1st Congressional District, which is now held by Davis and was redistricted to include more southern parts of the state, was one of the first majority-minority districts mandated by a 1982 amendment to the VRA that went into effect after the 1990 census.

“This 2026 election is different,” said Mikayla Massey, an organizer for the North Carolina Black Alliance. “Folks are seeing very clearly the dilution of the Black vote in North Carolina, and I think that that is motivating people in CD-1 and CD-3, and just on the ground in general, to be able to make sure that we come out, be too big to rig and still make our voices heard at the ballot box.”

College students in the state are holding “stroll to the poll” events for historically Black colleges and universities whose campuses lost early voting locations. Massey and a coalition of other organizations are also hosting education programs to inform voters about the changes to their districts and a hotline to support voters on Election Day.

Organizers say that momentum holds in Louisiana, where the Callais decision originated. Ashley Shelton, the president and CEO of the Power Coalition — a group of organizations that work to educate and empower voters — said that more Black voters turned out for the May election just days after the state Senate approved the revised map than they did in the 2023 gubernatorial race.

“It's an unfortunate action that our Legislature took, but the people said, ‘We don't want this. We do not like this,’” Shelton said. “I think they made a miscalculation about what the impact of them doing this actually will mean for them, both this election cycle and certainly into 2027 when all of them are back on the ballot.”
entries.author: Adora Brown

entries.title: After Jayden Daniels’ Latest Injury, the Commanders Have Tough Questions to Answer
entries.summary: Washington may not be able to count on its young quarterback in the long term.
entries.content:
ARLINGTON, Texas — Three seconds left in the first half, down a touchdown, ball on the Dallas Cowboys’ one-yard line, the Washington Commanders, as NFL teams tend to do, opted to put the ball and their immediate fate in the hands of their best player. In that moment, before it all unraveled in gruesome, stomach-churning fashion, the decision to eschew the easy field goal and go for seven points behind quarterback Jayden Daniels was curious but defensible.

“We needed touchdowns,” Commanders coach Dan Quinn said on Sunday following the 37-20 loss. “I don’t regret the call.”

In the immediate aftermath of the elbow dislocation that ended Daniels’s game, if not a large chunk of his season, the first reaction was some combination of horror and sadness. On the Fox telecast, where the image of Daniels’s fateful joint in a state of grotesque contortion was replayed over and over, color commentator Tom Brady spoke for the entire sport when he blurted, “Oh, shit.”

The next instinct, though, was to assign blame. Quinn, some were quick to say, should have taken the easy points instead of gambling with the health of his franchise quarterback. Right guard Chris Paul should have taken greater care not to step on Daniels’ foot after the snap, as the latter was trying to backpedal into position to throw. Somebody, anybody, should have done something, anything.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

But that stance fails to account for one of the fundamental truths about the NFL: On any given play on any given Sunday, there are 22 human brains, 44 knees, 44 elbows and 220 fingers susceptible to all manner of violent mangling. Daniels’s injury — a non-fractured dislocation, similar to the one he suffered to the same elbow last November, eventually ending his 2025 season — was no more likely to have happened on the play in question than on any other of his 16 previous pass attempts Sunday, or the 718 previous ones in his career.

“Obviously, anytime someone is injured you play the ‘What if?’ game,” Quinn said. “I don’t think this is one of those times for me.”

In hindsight, the moments prior to Daniels’s latest injury — the 0-1 Commanders on the cusp of tying a game in which they had trailed at one point by two touchdowns, with the second-half kickoff coming their way, the home opener at Northwest Stadium still a week away — were the last moments when there was still something resembling real, tangible hope for this Commanders season.

After a slow start in the Week 1 loss at Philadelphia, where the Commanders lost a winnable game thanks to a handful of crushing mistakes, Daniels was back to playing the way he did in 2024, when he was the NFL’s offensive rookie of the year and the Commanders were unlikely entrants in the NFC championship game. He was 11 of 16 for 96 passing yards and a touchdown as he awaited the snap at the end on the last play of Sunday’s first half, with another 69 yards on the ground.

He was electric. He was decisive with the ball. For the first time, he seemed to have a mastery of the new offense installed by first-year coordinator David Blough. He had put in the work to not only get back on the field after last year’s slog, but to be back at his best. And now, he was reaping the rewards.

But to see Daniels writhing on the turf at the end of the first half, his teammates kneeling around him, the medical cart summoned from the bowels of the stadium, was to see the beginning of the end.

By the time this slugfest ended, the Commanders’ injury report was bloated with names, and the reality of their plight was painfully obvious. At 0-2, with the defending Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks awaiting them next Sunday, they still have 88 percent of their season to play, and there is no telling how much of it, if any, will feature Daniels as their signal-caller. At least for the short term, prepare to see a lot of veteran backup Marcus Mariota under center.

“They’re definitely hurting for him,” Quinn said of his squad’s reaction to Daniels’s injury. “But … we will rally so hard around Marcus until Jayden is back. That’s what’s required, and that’s what we’ll do. And I expect our posture and attitude to reflect that.”

Mariota, a five-year starter earlier in his career and the man who finished out the 2025 season for the Commanders, might be absolutely fine as Daniels’s replacement, but he can’t do anything about the porous Washington secondary that Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott (who is now 13-2 in his career against the Commanders) carved up for 279 passing yards and four touchdowns, or the porous Washington offensive line that was already short-handed before starting guard Sam Cosmi suffered a brutal blow to the head that landed him in concussion protocol.

At a certain point, the questions about what happened to Daniels on Sunday are less about the position the Commanders placed him in, and more about Daniels himself: Will he ever make it through another NFL season unscathed? Can this franchise count on him in the long term?

He has played three games at AT&T Stadium in his career now, and he has failed to finish any of them. When will be the fourth? What gruesome end will be awaiting him then? And whose fault will it be that time?
entries.author: Dave Sheinin

entries.title: How ‘Corruption’ Took Over the Midterms
entries.summary: It’s a bipartisan theme across the most competitive House and Senate races: Political corruption is what’s really got you down.
entries.content:
Corruption is everywhere in New Hampshire’s competitive Senate race.

Republicans in the state are hammering Rep. Chris Pappas’ for being married to a former lobbyist, accusing the congressman of casting votes “on Amazon’s behalf.” Democrats, meanwhile, are attacking John Sununu, the former senator, for “cashing in” by “helping big pharma and big oil make billions, while we pay the price.”

This pair of ads represent dozens of campaign spots, backed by millions of dollars in spending, that zero in on corruption. It’s becoming the central line of attack in the 2026 midterms, with both parties opting for it as their main cudgel.

“We’re seeing more of these kinds of ads than ever before,” said Robert Blizzard, a Republican pollster. “It’s across every age group, income level, a feeling that they’re getting screwed but the stock market is somehow high, so the frustration with politics-as-usual, the assumed corruption that goes along with that, is at a fever pitch.”

Interviews with a dozen strategists from both parties, as well as private polling shared with The Washington Sun, reveal how anti-corruption campaigning has fundamentally changed this year. The messaging has long been popular with voters — but it didn’t necessarily determine their ultimate vote. This cycle, however, with an acutely frustrated electorate that blames both parties for what they see as a corrupt system, there’s an opening, these strategists said. It depends on linking political corruption to the voters’ own financial circumstances, turning it from an ethical problem into a financial one.

“As the candidate, you have to make clear that you’re going to take on corruption in both parties, including your own, and then you have to tie that corruption to costs going up for the voter, because what changes voting behavior is demonstrating the impact on them,” said Angie Kuefler, a Democratic pollster who has regularly briefed super PACs and campaigns on her corruption-related research. “Tying a bad, corrupt politician to rising costs is a double whammy, one-two punch, that connects to both the problem in politics and to their pain.”

The ads follow a similar script: Costs are rising because the opposing politician is taking donations from special interests, which then receive the green light to raise prices, on issues ranging from utilities to health care bills, while the politician turns a blind eye.

President Donald Trump doesn’t often get name-checked by Democrats in their corruption-centric ads against Republicans. But Democratic operatives argued that Trump’s personal enrichment in his second term has elevated the issue in the broader political environment. Trump’s self-dealing has reminded voters about what they dislike about a political system, they added, and has begun frustrating more than just Democratic voters.

“Trump, and his corruption, is baked in on everything, which is why the corruption piece is so good,” said one Democratic consultant who works on congressional races, who was granted anonymity to speak candidly. “You can link it directly to the candidates, and not make our ads just be about being anti-Trump.”

Or as one Democratic pollster said of the Trump administration: “They pushed it too far and pushed it past where normal voters are willing to put up with it.”

But the same pollster cautioned that Democrats have their own vulnerabilities on waste, fraud and abuse — particularly the Covid-era welfare fraud scandal in Minnesota.

“Corruption is an issue that cuts both ways,” said the pollster, who was granted anonymity to speak about the issue candidly.

Several strategists cited 2006 as the last midterm cycle to focus so much on corruption, a year defined by the Jack Abramoff lobbying scandal. But private Democratic research into how voters view corruption de-emphasized individual criminal corruption and fixed on legal, system-wide problems instead.

One research memo, produced for a Democratic super PAC and shared with The Sun, found that 52% of voters said the “most harmful” corruption involves “special interests, billionaires … acting within the law” to elect leaders who are beholden to them over "politicians breaking the law.” A third of those polled said criminal acts by individual politicians were more harmful than the influence of special interests.

And of white, non-college educated voters — a key demographic for both parties — 47% blamed the system over individual politicians.

Corruption is featured in TV ads in more than a dozen House races.

Republican ads hammer Rep. Vicente Gonzalez (D-Texas) for lavish travel “paid for by special interests” and Rep. Marcy Kaptur (D-Ohio) for steering money to defense contractors, after “taking tens of thousands” from them. Democratic ads hit former Iowa state Rep. Joe Mitchell for voting to “expand tax credits for developers,” then “his real estate companies pocketed more than $3 million,” and Rep. Rob Bresnahan (R-Pennsylvania) for being “caught selling stocks around his own votes.”

In some races, like in Colorado’s 8th Congressional District, Republicans and Democrats have released dueling ads accusing each other of selling out voters. House Majority PAC, the flagship Democratic super PAC, is attacking Rep. Gabe Evans (R-Colorado) for “slashing health care” while being “bankrolled by the health insurance industry.” The Congressional Leadership Fund, the prominent GOP super PAC, is up with an ad dinging former Democratic state Rep. Manny Rutinel for voting to get “automatic pay increases” in the state legislature while “you struggle to pay your bills.”

The messaging is even more prevalent in the Senate. In nearly every state with a competitive race — including New Hampshire, North Carolina, Ohio, Maine, Alaska, Michigan, Iowa, Texas and Minnesota — at least one candidate has recently run a corruption ad.

“I think there’s bipartisan anger that’s helped this bubble up to the surface,” said Calvin Moore, a Republican strategist. “It’s making the question in the race more about the individual candidates and their records, rather than an ideological argument, which puts more voters on the table.”

Political strategists emphasize that a direct message about affordability remains the top issue in the election. And both parties have poured millions of dollars into ads that focus on data centers, the Iran War and culture-war red meat.

But Democratic strategists interviewed by The Sun said repeatedly that they considered corruption a top three issue this year. And Republicans say the issue can play a key role in combatting a difficult political environment, training focus on local issues instead of voters’ misgivings about the direction of the country.

The red-leaning congressional map — where Kamala Harris only won three of the 40 or so most competitive House districts in the 2024 campaign — forces both parties “to reach across traditional partisan lines and talk about issues that are more character-based, rather than issue-based,” Blizzard, the GOP pollster, said.

For Democrats, it’s a matter of math. They have to win over at least some Republican-leaning voters. And for Republicans, “the political environment is so toxic for Republicans right now, your job is to remind Republican voters, who are depressed in these red districts and states, that these candidates are unacceptable alternatives,” Blizzard said.

It’s a rare message that unites voters of all backgrounds and ideologies in anger that can ricochet across party lines.

“Institutional members of Congress are very vulnerable to this because it’s a horseshoe-shaped issue that works well with voters in both parties,” said Rob Stutzman, a California-based Republican strategist. “Voters are in a zero tolerance mode for this.”
